background.definition: Diaper dermatitis (also known as diaper rash or napkin dermatitis or "nappy rash") is a nonspecific term that refers to any inflammatory eruption of the skin that occurs in the diaper area. Primary diaper dermatitis usually represents a form of irritant contact dermatitis, but secondary forms of dermatitis with defined etiologies are also possible.

list.listitem: The most common dermatologic problem of infancy.
Peak incidence typically reported as 9 to 12 months.
No difference in incidence by gender or race.
Although 5% to 6% have met criteria for a severe rash in earlier studies, this frequency appears to be decreasing.

A prevalence of 50% of all children at some stage of infancy in a 1986 survey, 25% of infants in a 1997 survey, and 16% in a 2007 survey of hospitalized children suggests that the frequency of this condition may be declining.
Rarely a severe or life-threatening condition (although case reports of fatal systemic fungal infection originating as a primary diaper dermatitis have been published for preterm infants).
Responsible for discomfort in infants and considerable caregiver anxiety.
Responsible for considerable financial costs (barrier creams, increased frequency of diaper changes or changing diaper brands, doctor visits, and prescription creams).
Multifactorial : see Pathophysiology
Most commonly: irritant contact from diaper contents
Commonly: opportunistic fungal infection (Candida spp.)
Less commonly: secondary bacterial infection (S. Aureus)
Rarely: underlying seborrheic dermatitis or psoriasis, other bacterial infection, other skin condition (eg, epidermolysis bullosa), or allergic dermatitis to diapers
Moist occlusion following urination in the diaper overhydrates the skin. Prolonged skin wetness predisposes it to mechanical injury, particularly the effects of friction.

Skin pH increases as fecal bacteria produce ammonia from urinary urea. Changed pH increases skin permeability to irritants and increases fecal enzyme activity. Increased stool proteases and lipases from feces also contribute to the erythema and epidermal barrier disruption of the skin. Microbes are not considered to play a primary role in the development of diaper dermatitis.

The above-mentioned factors cause an irritant contact dermatitis, which worsens with prolonged exposure. They may also predispose to opportunistic infection by fecal microbes, particularly Candida albicans, which causes a more severe and chronic dermatitis. More rarely bacterial infection with S. Aureus or Strep species may occur.
Rarely, allergy or other skin disorders are responsible for diaper dermatitis.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Lack of use of barrier cream

The use of breathable, superabsorbent disposable diapers causes less diaper dermatitis than non-breathable disposable diapers A and appears to prevent more severe forms of diaper dermatitis than reusable cloth diapers (usually with an overlying plastic pant). B

There are an increasing number of commercially available smartphone compatible remote moisture detection devices or temperature sensors being marketed to parents to prompt them to change a diaper once an infant has urinated with the goal of preventing diaper dermatitis although compelling evidence of efficacy is lacking. Most infants with moderate to severe dermatitis present for more than 3 days will have superinfection with Candida albicans. B

list.listitem: Diaper dermatitis can be classified clinically as either mild or moderate to severe.

Mild dermatitis is common and may not prompt a physician visit. The child is not sick and the mild rash often will respond to more diligent toileting practices and use of barrier creams. Mild dermatitis most typically represents simple irritant contact dermatitis and spares areas of the skin not in direct contact with the diaper and its contents, such as the flexures.

Physicians are more likely to be consulted for acute, or recurrent, moderate to severe dermatitis, where the child, although not systemically ill, may be uncomfortable. A more extensive red rash is noted throughout the diaper area, which may include beefy redness, satellite lesions, peeling skin, and ulceration.

Satellite lesions are discrete papular or pustular lesions at the margins of a rash. The presence of satellite lesions and rash within the flexures (noncontact areas) are highly suggestive of candidiasis.
Children with coexistent eczema will typically have dry skin elsewhere on their bodies and may have rash in the antecubital and popliteal fossae.

An allergic reaction to plastic or rubber within the diaper is suggested by rash occurring predominantly over both inguinal areas that come in contact with the adhesive tabs of disposable diapers or along the margins of the diaper area where plastic pants are worn over a cloth diaper.
Other features suggestive of less common etiologies are listed under the differential diagnosis section.

Theoretically, KOH testing might assist in diagnosing opportunistic fungal infection. However, given the high prevalence of candidiasis in moderate to severe diaper dermatitis (75% colonization noted in one study); empiric treatment with anti-fungal therapy is instead recommended without diagnostic confirmation.

Rapid antigen testing or culture for β-hemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis should be considered in management of acute diaper dermatitis when systemic illness suggests that an acute streptococcal infection may be present.
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to management.

The application of an over-the-counter barrier paste (in particular one containing zinc oxide and starch in a greasy vehicle such as petrolatum or soft paraffin) to the infant's diaper area after each diaper change is recommended. C
For moderate to severe dermatitis, given the high likelihood of Candida infection, strongly consider prescribing an antifungal cream. A
Add a topical low-potency corticosteroid cream for moderate to severe dermatitis. A
Preparations that combine antifungals with high-potency steroids (such as betamethasone dipropionate present in Lotrisone) should be avoided. C
The addition of an oral antifungal does not improve outcome and is not recommended. A
Mupirocin ointment or 2% eosin solution are effective antifungal agents and can be used. A

The application of an over-the-counter barrier paste (in particular one containing zinc oxide and starch in a greasy vehicle such as petrolatum or soft paraffin) to the infant's diaper area after each diaper change is recommended.
Add a topical low-potency corticosteroid cream for moderate to severe dermatitis.

Given the high likelihood of Candida infection, strongly consider prescribing an antifungal cream. However, preparations that combine antifungals with high-potency steroids (such as betamethasone dipropionate present in Lotrisone) should be avoided.

listitem.strong: Persistent or recurrent moderate to severe diaper dermatitis

list.listitem: Confirm and reinforce that the good diaper changing practices outlined above are being followed.
If not yet used, consider topical mupirocin ointment or 2% eosin solution.

Consider the coexistence of systemic or other dermopathies, most commonly eczema and treat or refer accordingly. Consider whether more rare etiologies may be present, and whether caregiver neglect or abuse may be occurring.
A wide range of creams and pastes may be used, the majority of which are lacking in evidence of effectiveness.

A cohort study of 12 infants with moderate to severe rash followed for 7 days reported that a blend of natural honey, olive oil, and beeswax massaged into the perineum 4 times daily resulted in no or mild diaper rash at 7 days in 10 of the children.
Because vitamin A deficiency can cause skin disease, creams containing vitamin A are often promoted for diaper dermatitis. However, there is no evidence to support their effectiveness.
An RCT of 90 newborns followed for 4 months found that oral zinc supplementation significantly reduced the incidence of diaper rash compared with placebo. Good safety data are lacking, though.

Apart from rare cases with atypical etiology or its occurrence in hospitalized, very-low-birth-weight infants, diaper dermatitis is a self-limiting condition with an excellent prognosis that does not result in severe illness or permanent sequelae. B

cell.label: Assess severity: <10% diaper area affected, faint to mild pink color, few or no satellite lesions, no ulceration, child is not distressed?

Mild diaper dermatitis Leave skin exposed as much as possible, frequent diaper changes, use fragrance-free, alcohol-free wipes or water to clean and avoid soaps or perfumed products, and apply a barrier paste (zinc oxide) at each diaper change.

Moderate/severe diaper dermatitis Treatment for mild diaper dermatitis, plus: (1) topical antifungal preparation (nystatin cream BID-TID), (2) topical corticosteroid (1% hydrocortisone cream BID), and (3) consider mupirocin or eosin.
Confirms diagnosis, minimize recurrence by continuing treatment for mild diaper dermatitis.
Ensure adequate treatment of opportunistic fungal infection; consider underlying skin disorder, such as eczema; consider alternate diagnoses.

footnotes.footnote: For moderate-severe dermatitis, opportunistic infection with Candida is likely. Although unsupported by evidence, a blend of Aquaphor ointment (4 parts), stomahesive paste (2 parts), and nystatin cream (1 part) compounded by a pharmacist as "butt paste"; is often prescribed, with anecdotal benefits.
